claim: Meiotic recombination is a fundamental genetic process that generates new combinations of alleles on which natural selection can act.
source: Meiotic recombination is a fundamental genetic process that generates new combinations of alleles on which natural selection can act and, in most sexually-reproducing organisms, plays critical roles in the proper alignment and segregation of homologous chromosomes during meiosis (Coop and Przeworski, 2007; de Massy, 2013; Lam and Keeney, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coop and Przeworski, 2007; de Massy, 2013; Lam and Keeney, 2014

claim: In most sexually-reproducing organisms, meiotic recombination plays critical roles in the proper alignment and segregation of homologous chromosomes during meiosis.
source: Meiotic recombination is a fundamental genetic process that generates new combinations of alleles on which natural selection can act and, in most sexually-reproducing organisms, plays critical roles in the proper alignment and segregation of homologous chromosomes during meiosis (Coop and Przeworski, 2007; de Massy, 2013; Lam and Keeney, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coop and Przeworski, 2007; de Massy, 2013; Lam and Keeney, 2014

claim: Meiotic recombination is initiated by a set of double strand breaks (DSBs) deliberately inflicted throughout the genome.
source: Meiotic recombination is initiated by a set of double strand breaks (DSBs) deliberately inflicted throughout the genome, whose repair leads to crossover and non-crossover recombination events (Lam and Keeney, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lam and Keeney, 2014

claim: Repair of double strand breaks leads to crossover and non-crossover recombination events.
source: Meiotic recombination is initiated by a set of double strand breaks (DSBs) deliberately inflicted throughout the genome, whose repair leads to crossover and non-crossover recombination events (Lam and Keeney, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lam and Keeney, 2014

claim: Most of the molecular machinery involved in meiotic recombination in vertebrates has been conserved since the common ancestor of plants, animals and fungi.
source: Most of the molecular machinery involved in this process in vertebrates has been conserved since the common ancestor of plants, animals and fungi (de Massy, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Massy, 2013

claim: In all sexually reproducing species that have been examined, the SPO11 protein generates DSBs.
source: Notably, in all sexually reproducing species that have been examined, the SPO11 protein generates DSBs, which localize to histone H3 lysine K4 trimethylation marks (H3K4me3) along the genome (Borde et al., 2009; Buard et al., 2009; Lam and Keeney, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Borde et al., 2009; Buard et al., 2009; Lam and Keeney, 2014

claim: DSBs localize to histone H3 lysine K4 trimethylation marks (H3K4me3) along the genome.
source: Notably, in all sexually reproducing species that have been examined, the SPO11 protein generates DSBs, which localize to histone H3 lysine K4 trimethylation marks (H3K4me3) along the genome (Borde et al., 2009; Buard et al., 2009; Lam and Keeney, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Borde et al., 2009; Buard et al., 2009; Lam and Keeney, 2014

claim: In many species, including all yeast, plant and vertebrate species studied to date, recombination events are localized to short intervals known as recombination hotspots.
source: As one example, in many species, including all yeast, plant and vertebrate species studied to date, recombination events are localized to short intervals (of hundreds to thousands of base pairs; Lange et al., 2016) known as recombination hotspots, whereas in others, such as in flies or worms, the recombination landscape seems more uniform, lacking such hotspots (Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009; Chan et al., 2012; Heil et al. 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lange et al., 2016

claim: Recombination hotspots span hundreds to thousands of base pairs.
source: As one example, in many species, including all yeast, plant and vertebrate species studied to date, recombination events are localized to short intervals (of hundreds to thousands of base pairs; Lange et al., 2016) known as recombination hotspots, whereas in others, such as in flies or worms, the recombination landscape seems more uniform, lacking such hotspots (Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009; Chan et al., 2012; Heil et al. 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lange et al., 2016

claim: In flies and worms, the recombination landscape seems more uniform, lacking hotspots.
source: As one example, in many species, including all yeast, plant and vertebrate species studied to date, recombination events are localized to short intervals (of hundreds to thousands of base pairs; Lange et al., 2016) known as recombination hotspots, whereas in others, such as in flies or worms, the recombination landscape seems more uniform, lacking such hotspots (Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009; Chan et al., 2012; Heil et al. 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009; Chan et al., 2012; Heil et al. 2015

claim: In mammalian species, including apes, mice and likely cattle, the locations of recombination hotspots are specified by PRDM9 binding.
source: In mammalian species, including apes, mice and likely cattle, the locations of recombination hotspots are specified by PRDM9 binding (Baudat et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010; Sandor et al., 2012; Great Ape Genome Project et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baudat et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010; Sandor et al., 2012; Great Ape Genome Project et al., 2016

claim: PRDM9 has four major functional domains: a KRAB, SSXRD and PR/SET domain, followed by a C2H2 zinc finger (ZF) array.
source: In these species, PRDM9 has four major functional domains: a KRAB, SSXRD and PR/SET domain (referred to as the SET domain in what follows), followed by a C2H2 zinc finger (ZF) array (Figure 1).
evidence: Directly stated in text and shown in Figure 1

claim: During meiosis, PRDM9 binds sequences throughout the genome, as specified by its ZF array.
source: During meiosis, PRDM9 binds sequences throughout the genome, as specified by its ZF array (reviewed in Ségurel et al., 2011), and the SET domain of PRDM9 makes H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks nearby (Eram et al., 2014; Powers et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ségurel et al., 2011

claim: The SET domain of PRDM9 makes H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks nearby its binding sites.
source: During meiosis, PRDM9 binds sequences throughout the genome, as specified by its ZF array (reviewed in Ségurel et al., 2011), and the SET domain of PRDM9 makes H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 marks nearby (Eram et al., 2014; Powers et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eram et al., 2014; Powers et al., 2016

claim: PRDM9 actions serve to recruit SPO11 to initiate DSBs.
source: These actions ultimately serve to recruit SPO11 to initiate DSBs, by a mechanism that remains unknown but is associated with the presence of both histone marks (Grey et al., 2017; Getun et al., 2017) and may involve KRAB and SSXRD domains (Parvanov et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grey et al., 2017; Getun et al., 2017; Parvanov et al., 2017

claim: The mechanism by which PRDM9 recruits SPO11 is associated with the presence of both H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 histone marks.
source: These actions ultimately serve to recruit SPO11 to initiate DSBs, by a mechanism that remains unknown but is associated with the presence of both histone marks (Grey et al., 2017; Getun et al., 2017) and may involve KRAB and SSXRD domains (Parvanov et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grey et al., 2017; Getun et al., 2017

claim: The mechanism by which PRDM9 recruits SPO11 may involve KRAB and SSXRD domains.
source: These actions ultimately serve to recruit SPO11 to initiate DSBs, by a mechanism that remains unknown but is associated with the presence of both histone marks (Grey et al., 2017; Getun et al., 2017) and may involve KRAB and SSXRD domains (Parvanov et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parvanov et al., 2017, but described as speculative

claim: In vertebrate species such as birds and canids that lack functional PRDM9 orthologs, recombination events are concentrated at or near promoter-like features, including TSSs and CpG islands.
source: In contrast, in yeasts, plants, and vertebrate species (such as birds and canids) that lack functional PRDM9 orthologs, recombination events are concentrated at or near promoter-like features, including TSSs and CpG islands (CGIs), perhaps because they are associated with greater chromatin accessibility (Lichten and Goldman, 1995; Auton et al., 2013; Choi et al., 2013; Hellsten et al., 2013; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Singhal et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lichten and Goldman, 1995; Auton et al., 2013; Choi et al., 2013; Hellsten et al., 2013; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Singhal et al., 2015

claim: Recombination concentration at promoter-like features in species lacking PRDM9 may be because they are associated with greater chromatin accessibility.
source: In contrast, in yeasts, plants, and vertebrate species (such as birds and canids) that lack functional PRDM9 orthologs, recombination events are concentrated at or near promoter-like features, including TSSs and CpG islands (CGIs), perhaps because they are associated with greater chromatin accessibility (Lichten and Goldman, 1995; Auton et al., 2013; Choi et al., 2013; Hellsten et al., 2013; Lam and Keeney, 2015; Singhal et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citations

claim: In mouse knockouts for PRDM9, recombination events appear to default to promoter-like features that carry H3K4me3 peaks.
source: Similarly, in mouse knockouts for PRDM9, recombination events appear to default to promoter-like features that carry H3K4me3 peaks (Brick et al., 2012; Narasimhan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brick et al., 2012; Narasimhan et al., 2016

claim: When recombination is directed by PRDM9, hotspot locations are not shared between closely related ape species or between mouse subspecies.
source: When recombination is directed by PRDM9, hotspot locations are not shared between closely related ape species or between mouse subspecies and differ even among human populations (Ptak et al., 2004; Myers et al., 2005; Ptak et al., 2005; Coop et al., 2008; Hinch et al., 2011; Auton et al., 2012; Great Ape Genome Project et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ptak et al., 2004; Myers et al., 2005; Ptak et al., 2005; Coop et al., 2008; Hinch et al., 2011; Auton et al., 2012; Great Ape Genome Project et al., 2016

claim: Hotspot locations differ even among human populations.
source: When recombination is directed by PRDM9, hotspot locations are not shared between closely related ape species or between mouse subspecies and differ even among human populations (Ptak et al., 2004; Myers et al., 2005; Ptak et al., 2005; Coop et al., 2008; Hinch et al., 2011; Auton et al., 2012; Great Ape Genome Project et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ptak et al., 2004; Myers et al., 2005; Ptak et al., 2005; Coop et al., 2008; Hinch et al., 2011; Auton et al., 2012; Great Ape Genome Project et al., 2016

claim: The binding specificity of the PRDM9 ZF leads to the existence of 'hotter' and 'colder' alleles.
source: First, the binding specificity of the PRDM9 ZF leads to the existence of 'hotter' and 'colder' alleles, that is, sequences that are more or less likely to be bound by PRDM9 (Myers et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Myers et al., 2008

claim: In heterozygotes carrying a colder and a hotter allele, the hotter alleles more often experience a DSB.
source: In heterozygotes carrying a colder and a hotter allele, this asymmetry in binding leads to the hotter alleles more often experiencing a DSB (Baker et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baker et al., 2015; Davies et al., 2016

claim: Repair mechanisms use the intact, colder allele as a template, leading to preferential loss of sequences to which PRDM9 binds.
source: Since repair mechanisms use the intact, colder allele as a template, the sequences to which PRDM9 binds are preferentially lost (Boulton et al., 1997; Kauppi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boulton et al., 1997; Kauppi et al., 2005

claim: Under-transmission of the hotter allele in hot/cold heterozygotes acts analogously to selection for the colder allele.
source: This process of under-transmission of the hotter allele in hot/cold heterozygotes acts analogously to selection for the colder allele (Nagylaki and Petes, 1982) and is thus expected to drive the rapid loss of hotspots from the population (leading to the 'hotspot paradox'; Pineda-Krch and Redfield, 2005; Coop and Myers, 2007), consistent with empirical observations in humans and mice (Berg et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2010; Baker et al., 2015; Smagulova et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nagylaki and Petes, 1982; Pineda-Krch and Redfield, 2005; Coop and Myers, 2007; Berg et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2010; Baker et al., 2015; Smagulova et al., 2016

claim: PRDM9 has the fastest evolving C2H2 ZF array in the mouse and human genomes.
source: Interestingly, PRDM9 has the fastest evolving C2H2 ZF array in the mouse and human genomes (Oliver et al., 2009; Myers et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oliver et al., 2009; Myers et al., 2010

claim: Mammalian PRDM9 genes show strong evidence of positive selection at known DNA-binding sites of ZFs.
source: More generally, mammalian PRDM9 genes show strong evidence of positive selection at known DNA-binding sites of ZFs (Oliver et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oliver et al., 2009

claim: In birds that lack an ortholog of PRDM9, the locations of recombination hotspots are conserved over long evolutionary time scales.
source: In birds that lack an ortholog of PRDM9, the locations of recombination hotspots are conserved over long evolutionary time scales.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Both the location and heats of recombination hotspots are conserved across highly diverged yeast species.
source: Similarly, both the location and heats of recombination hotspots are conserved across highly diverged yeast species, in which H3K4me3 marks are made by a single gene without a DNA binding domain (Lam and Keeney, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lam and Keeney, 2015

claim: The study identified 227 PRDM9 orthologs across vertebrates.
source: This approach identified 227 PRDM9 orthologs (Supplementary file 1A,B), found in jawless fish, cartilaginous fish, bony fish, coelacanths, turtles, snakes, lizards, and mammals.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: PRDM9 orthologs were found in jawless fish, cartilaginous fish, bony fish, coelacanths, turtles, snakes, lizards, and mammals.
source: This approach identified 227 PRDM9 orthologs (Supplementary file 1A,B), found in jawless fish, cartilaginous fish, bony fish, coelacanths, turtles, snakes, lizards, and mammals.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: The study confirmed the absence of PRDM9 in all sampled birds and crocodiles.
source: We confirmed the absence of PRDM9 in all sampled birds and crocodiles (Oliver et al., 2009; Singhal et al., 2015), the absence of non-pseudogene copies in canids (Oliver et al., 2009; Muñoz-Fuentes et al., 2011), and additionally were unable to identify PRDM9 genes in amphibians (Figure 1), despite targeted searches of whole genome sequences (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Confirmed by study analysis and supported by citations to Oliver et al., 2009; Singhal et al., 2015

claim: The study confirmed the absence of non-pseudogene copies of PRDM9 in canids.
source: We confirmed the absence of PRDM9 in all sampled birds and crocodiles (Oliver et al., 2009; Singhal et al., 2015), the absence of non-pseudogene copies in canids (Oliver et al., 2009; Muñoz-Fuentes et al., 2011), and additionally were unable to identify PRDM9 genes in amphibians (Figure 1), despite targeted searches of whole genome sequences (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Confirmed by study analysis and supported by citations to Oliver et al., 2009; Muñoz-Fuentes et al., 2011

claim: The study was unable to identify PRDM9 genes in amphibians despite targeted searches of whole genome sequences.
source: We confirmed the absence of PRDM9 in all sampled birds and crocodiles (Oliver et al., 2009; Singhal et al., 2015), the absence of non-pseudogene copies in canids (Oliver et al., 2009; Muñoz-Fuentes et al., 2011), and additionally were unable to identify PRDM9 genes in amphibians (Figure 1), despite targeted searches of whole genome sequences (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: An ancient duplication of PRDM9 occurred in the common ancestor of teleost fish, coincident with the whole genome duplication in this group.
source: We further inferred an ancient duplication of PRDM9 in the common ancestor of teleost fish, apparently coincident with the whole genome duplication that occurred in this group (Figure 1, Figure 2).
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figures 1 and 2

claim: The two PRDM9 copies in teleost fish are referred to as PRDM9α and PRDM9β.
source: We used both phylogenetic methods and analysis of the ZF structure to distinguish these copies (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods) and refer to them as PRDM9α and PRDM9β in what follows.
evidence: Directly stated as nomenclature used in the study

claim: PRDM9β orthologs were identified in each species of teleost fish examined.
source: While PRDM9β orthologs were identified in each species of teleost fish examined, we were unable to identify PRDM9α type orthologs within three major teleost taxa, suggesting at minimum three losses of PRDM9α type orthologs within teleost fish (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: At minimum three losses of PRDM9α type orthologs occurred within teleost fish.
source: While PRDM9β orthologs were identified in each species of teleost fish examined, we were unable to identify PRDM9α type orthologs within three major teleost taxa, suggesting at minimum three losses of PRDM9α type orthologs within teleost fish (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Inferred from absence of PRDM9α in three major teleost taxa

claim: PRDM9 orthologs identified in jawless fish, some bony fish, coelacanths, lizards, snakes, turtles, and placental mammals have a complete domain structure consisting of KRAB, SSXRD and SET domains, as well as a C2H2 ZF array.
source: PRDM9 orthologs identified in jawless fish, some bony fish, coelacanths, lizards, snakes, turtles, and placental mammals have a complete domain structure, consisting of KRAB, SSXRD and SET domains, as well as a C2H2 ZF array.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: A complete PRDM9 ortholog was present in the common ancestor of vertebrates.
source: The phylogenetic relationships between these species suggest that a complete PRDM9 ortholog was present in the common ancestor of vertebrates (Figure 1).
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic relationships shown in Figure 1

claim: The SSXRD domain is absent in some cartilaginous fish.
source: Instances include the absence of the SSXRD domain in some cartilaginous fish (see Materials and methods), absence of both KRAB and SSXRD domains in PRDM9β orthologs (Figure 1) and in PRDM9α orthologs found distributed throughout the teleost fish phylogeny (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and the absence of the KRAB domain in monotremata (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) and marsupial mammals (Sarcophilus harrisii, Figure 1; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: Both KRAB and SSXRD domains are absent in PRDM9β orthologs.
source: Instances include the absence of the SSXRD domain in some cartilaginous fish (see Materials and methods), absence of both KRAB and SSXRD domains in PRDM9β orthologs (Figure 1) and in PRDM9α orthologs found distributed throughout the teleost fish phylogeny (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and the absence of the KRAB domain in monotremata (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) and marsupial mammals (Sarcophilus harrisii, Figure 1; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 1

claim: The KRAB domain is absent in monotremata (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) and marsupial mammals (Sarcophilus harrisii).
source: Instances include the absence of the SSXRD domain in some cartilaginous fish (see Materials and methods), absence of both KRAB and SSXRD domains in PRDM9β orthologs (Figure 1) and in PRDM9α orthologs found distributed throughout the teleost fish phylogeny (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and the absence of the KRAB domain in monotremata (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) and marsupial mammals (Sarcophilus harrisii, Figure 1; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 1

claim: The study confirmed a minimum of six N-terminal domain losses within vertebrates.
source: This approach necessarily limits our ability to verify putative losses when there are no suitable transcriptome data, but nonetheless allowed us to confirm the losses of the KRAB and SSXRD domains in a PRDM9 ortholog from holostean fish (Lepisosteus oculatus), in all PRDM9β orthologs from teleost fish (Figure 1), in PRDM9α orthologs that lost their complete domain structure in several taxa of teleost fish (Gadus morhua, Astyanax mexicanus, Ictalurus punctatus, Esox lucius; Supplementary file 2C), as well as losses of the KRAB domain in two PRDM9 orthologs identified in monotremata (both in O. anatinus, Supplementary file 2C), indicating a minimum of six N-terminal domain losses within vertebrates.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: In all cases of N-terminal truncation examined, the partial PRDM9 shows evidence of functional constraint (dN/dS <1).
source: In all cases of N-terminal truncation, the partial PRDM9 shows evidence of functional constraint (i.e., dN/dS <1, where dN is the rate of amino-acid substitutions and dS of synonymous substitutions; see Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: A partial PRDM9 ortholog in teleost fish has been evolving under constraint for hundreds of millions of years.
source: This conservation is most strikingly seen in teleost fish, in which a partial PRDM9 ortholog has been evolving under constraint for hundreds of millions of years (Figure 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in figures

claim: Placental mammals that have PRDM9-directed recombination show exceptionally high rates of evolution of the PRDM9 ZF compared to other ZFs.
source: Using this statistic, placental mammals that have PRDM9-directed recombination show exceptionally high rates of evolution of the PRDM9 ZF compared to other ZFs (Table 1; Baudat et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2010; Parvanov et al., 2010).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Table 1, supported by citations

claim: Two of six cattle PRDM9 orthologs identified were previously associated with interspecific variation in recombination phenotypes.
source: Moreover, two of six cattle PRDM9 orthologs that we identified were previously associated with interspecific variation in recombination phenotypes (Supplementary file 3B; Sandor et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2015), and both are seen to be rapidly evolving (Table 1, Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis, supported by citations to Sandor et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2015

claim: PRDM9 orthologs in jawless fish, some bony fish (Salmoniformes, Esociformes, Elopomorpha), turtles, snakes, lizards, and coelacanths show elevated values of the rapid evolution statistic similar to placental mammals.
source: In addition to placental mammals, PRDM9 orthologs in jawless fish, some bony fish (Salmoniformes, Esociformes, Elopomorpha), turtles, snakes, lizards, and coelacanths show similarly elevated values of this statistic (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: PRDM9 is the most rapidly evolving ZF gene genome-wide in most species with complete domain structure.
source: In fact, PRDM9 is the most rapidly evolving ZF gene genome-wide in most species in these taxa and all PRDM9 orthologs with the complete domain structure were in the top 5% of the most rapidly evolving ZFs in their respective genomes (Table 1, Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Table 1

claim: All PRDM9 orthologs with the complete domain structure were in the top 5% of the most rapidly evolving ZFs in their respective genomes.
source: In fact, PRDM9 is the most rapidly evolving ZF gene genome-wide in most species in these taxa and all PRDM9 orthologs with the complete domain structure were in the top 5% of the most rapidly evolving ZFs in their respective genomes (Table 1, Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Table 1

claim: Evidence of rapid evolution is absent from PRDM9β orthologs and partial PRDM9α orthologs in bony fish.
source: In contrast, evidence of such rapid evolution is absent from other taxa of bony fish, including all PRDM9β orthologs and partial PRDM9α orthologs, as well as from the putatively partial PRDM9 orthologs found in the elephant shark, the Tasmanian devil, and in several species of placental mammals (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: Species show evidence of rapid evolution of the ZF binding affinity if and only if they carry the intact PRDM9 ortholog found in placental mammals, with one possible exception.
source: In summary, with one possible exception, species show evidence of rapid evolution of the ZF binding affinity if and only if they carry the intact PRDM9 ortholog found in placental mammals.
evidence: Directly stated as a summary of the study's findings

claim: The concordance of rapid evolution with the complete domain structure is highly unlikely by chance (p<10−6).
source: This concordance of rapid evolution with the complete domain structure is highly unlikely by chance (taking into account the phylogenetic relationship between orthologs, p<10−6; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of statistical analysis

claim: KRAB and SSXRD domains are required for PRDM9's role in directing recombination.
source: Assuming that rapid evolution of the ZF is indicative of PRDM9-directed recombination, these observations carry two implications: KRAB and SSXRD domains are required for this role and non-mammalian species such as turtles or snakes also use PRDM9 to direct recombination.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between complete domain structure and rapid ZF evolution

claim: Non-mammalian species such as turtles or snakes also use PRDM9 to direct recombination.
source: Assuming that rapid evolution of the ZF is indicative of PRDM9-directed recombination, these observations carry two implications: KRAB and SSXRD domains are required for this role and non-mammalian species such as turtles or snakes also use PRDM9 to direct recombination.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of complete PRDM9 and rapid ZF evolution in these species

claim: Three tyrosine residues (Y276, Y341 and Y357) are important for the catalytic specificities of the human PRDM9 gene.
source: Specifically, we focused on three tyrosine residues shown to be important for the catalytic specificities of the human PRDM9 gene (Y276, Y341 and Y357; see Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1A; Wu et al., 2013) and asked if those residues were conserved across vertebrates.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2013

claim: Each of the three catalytic residues (Y276, Y341 and Y357) is broadly conserved across the vertebrate phylogeny.
source: We found that each of the three residues is broadly conserved across the vertebrate phylogeny, with substitutions observed in only 57 of 227 PRDM9 orthologs, including 11 genes from placental mammals and 46 genes from bony fish.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: None of the substitutions at catalytic residues occur in a complete PRDM9 ortholog containing KRAB, SSXRD, SET and ZF domains.
source: Strikingly, however, none of these substitutions occur in a complete PRDM9 ortholog containing KRAB, SSXRD, SET and ZF domains.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: No substitutions were observed at catalytic residues in any PRDM9α ortholog, regardless of their domain architecture.
source: In contrast, no substitutions were observed at these residues in any PRDM9α ortholog, regardless of their domain architecture.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: Swordtail fish have testis-specific expression of a PRDM9β type gene that lacks the KRAB and SSXRD domains.
source: Like other percomorphs, swordtail fish have testis-specific expression of a PRDM9β type gene that lacks the KRAB and SSXRD domains, and has a slowly evolving ZF array (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1); they further carry substitutions at two catalytic residues of the SET domain (Y341F and Y357P), as well as at residues of the SET domain implicated in H3K4me2 recognition (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 4

claim: Swordtail fish PRDM9 has a slowly evolving ZF array.
source: Like other percomorphs, swordtail fish have testis-specific expression of a PRDM9β type gene that lacks the KRAB and SSXRD domains, and has a slowly evolving ZF array (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1); they further carry substitutions at two catalytic residues of the SET domain (Y341F and Y357P), as well as at residues of the SET domain implicated in H3K4me2 recognition (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 4

claim: Swordtail fish PRDM9 carries substitutions at two catalytic residues of the SET domain (Y341F and Y357P).
source: Like other percomorphs, swordtail fish have testis-specific expression of a PRDM9β type gene that lacks the KRAB and SSXRD domains, and has a slowly evolving ZF array (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1); they further carry substitutions at two catalytic residues of the SET domain (Y341F and Y357P), as well as at residues of the SET domain implicated in H3K4me2 recognition (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: In swordtail fish, recombination rates are elevated near TSSs and CGIs.
source: By this approach, we found recombination rates to be elevated near TSSs and CGIs, two promoter-like features (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 4

claim: In swordtail fish, there is no elevation in recombination rates near computationally-predicted PRDM9 binding sites.
source: Moreover, and in contrast to what is observed in species with PRDM9-mediated recombination (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), there is no elevation in recombination rates near computationally-predicted PRDM9 binding sites (Figure 4F).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 4F

claim: Recombination patterns in swordtail fish resemble those previously reported for birds lacking PRDM9.
source: These patterns resemble those previously reported for birds lacking PRDM9 (Singhal et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison to published data, supported by citation to Singhal et al., 2015

claim: In swordtail fish, recombination is increased around H3K4me3 peaks.
source: Consistent with a role for H3K4me3 in inducing DSBs, recombination is increased around H3K4me3 peaks (testing the association with distance, rho = −0.072, p=2.3e-69; Figure 4), an effect that remains significant after correcting for distance to TSSs and CGIs (rho = −0.026, p=5.4e-10).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis with statistical support and shown in Figure 4

claim: In swordtail fish, windows that contain testis-specific H3K4me3 peaks have significantly higher recombination rates than those that contain liver-specific H3K4me3 peaks.
source: Windows that contain testis-specific H3K4me3 peaks have significantly higher recombination rates than those that contain liver-specific H3K4me3 peaks (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 4

claim: In swordtail fish, H3K4me3 peaks in the testis are not enriched for the computationally predicted PRDM9 motifs.
source: However, H3K4me3 peaks in the testis are not enriched for the computationally predicted PRDM9 motifs (Figure 4), nor do they overlap with PRDM9 motifs in the testis more than the liver (see Methods).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 4

claim: In swordtail fish, sequence motifs associated with testis-specific H3K4me3 peaks do not resemble the predicted PRDM9 motif.
source: Conversely, sequence motifs associated with testis-specific H3K4me3 peaks do not resemble the predicted PRDM9 motif (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 4

claim: There is no evidence that PRDM9 lays down the H3K4me3 marks associated with an increase in recombination in swordtails.
source: Thus, there is no evidence that PRDM9 lays down the H3K4me3 marks associated with an increase in recombination in swordtails.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing no association between PRDM9 motifs and H3K4me3 peaks or recombination

claim: Among species with complete PRDM9 genes, recombination rates are either weakly reduced near TSSs and CGIs or similar to what is seen in nearby windows.
source: Among species with complete PRDM9 genes, recombination rates are either weakly reduced near TSSs and CGIs or similar to what is seen in nearby windows (Figure 5; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for results with genetic maps based on pedigrees or admixture switches instead of LD data in humans and dogs).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 5

claim: In all species lacking PRDM9 and in swordtail fish, the recombination rate is notably increased in windows overlapping either a TSS or CGI relative to nearby windows.
source: In contrast, in all species lacking PRDM9 and in swordtail fish, the recombination rate is notably increased in windows overlapping either a TSS or CGI relative to nearby windows.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: Patterns of recombination near TSSs and CGIs differ between species carrying complete PRDM9 orthologs and species lacking PRDM9 altogether.
source: Nonetheless, these results indicate that patterns of recombination near TSSs and CGIs differ between species carrying complete PRDM9 orthologs and species lacking PRDM9 altogether, and that swordtail fish exhibit patterns of recombination similar to species that completely lack PRDM9, despite the presence of a partial ortholog.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion from the study's analysis

claim: Swordtail fish exhibit patterns of recombination similar to species that completely lack PRDM9, despite the presence of a partial ortholog.
source: Nonetheless, these results indicate that patterns of recombination near TSSs and CGIs differ between species carrying complete PRDM9 orthologs and species lacking PRDM9 altogether, and that swordtail fish exhibit patterns of recombination similar to species that completely lack PRDM9, despite the presence of a partial ortholog.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion from the study's analysis

claim: The ancestral domain architecture of PRDM9 consisted of KRAB, SSXRD and SET domains followed by a C2H2 ZF array.
source: Based on our reconstruction of 227 PRDM9 orthologs across the vertebrate phylogeny, we inferred that the ancestral domain architecture of PRDM9 consisted of KRAB, SSXRD and SET domains followed by a C2H2 ZF array, and that this complete architecture was likely already in place in the common ancestor of vertebrates.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic reconstruction of 227 PRDM9 orthologs

claim: The complete PRDM9 architecture was likely already in place in the common ancestor of vertebrates.
source: Based on our reconstruction of 227 PRDM9 orthologs across the vertebrate phylogeny, we inferred that the ancestral domain architecture of PRDM9 consisted of KRAB, SSXRD and SET domains followed by a C2H2 ZF array, and that this complete architecture was likely already in place in the common ancestor of vertebrates.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic reconstruction of 227 PRDM9 orthologs

claim: All four domains of PRDM9 are important for its function.
source: Moreover, even though to date only the functions of the SET domain and C2H2 ZF array have been connected to the role of PRDM9 in directing recombination, the evolutionary patterns uncovered here suggest that all four domains are important.
evidence: Inferred from evolutionary patterns observed in the study

claim: Swordtail fish with a truncated copy of PRDM9 missing KRAB and SSXRD domains behave like PRDM9 knockouts in their fine-scale recombination patterns.
source: The second piece of evidence is that swordtail fish with a truncated copy of PRDM9 that is missing KRAB and SSXRD domains behave like PRDM9 knockouts in their fine-scale recombination patterns.
evidence: Directly stated as a conclusion from the study's analysis of swordtail fish recombination patterns

claim: Substitutions at catalytic residues are only seen in PRDM9 genes that have lost KRAB and/or SSXRD domains or have lost the ZF entirely.
source: However, substitutions at catalytic residues are only seen in PRDM9 genes that have lost KRAB and/or SSXRD domains or have lost the ZF entirely.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis

claim: The absence of KRAB and SSXRD domains in a PRDM9 ortholog may signify that PRDM9 is no longer used to direct recombination.
source: We speculate that the absence of KRAB and SSXRD domains in a PRDM9 ortholog may similarly signify that PRDM9 is no longer used to direct recombination and lead to reduced constraint on the catalytic activities of the SET domain.
evidence: Speculative inference from the observed patterns

claim: A recent paper suggests that the KRAB domain may play a role in recruiting the recombination machinery.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, a recent paper suggests that the KRAB domain may play a role in recruiting the recombination machinery (Parvanov et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Parvanov et al., 2017

claim: The overall conservation of partial PRDM9 orthologs points to another role of the gene.
source: If the partial ortholog of PRDM9 is not used to direct recombination at all, then the overall conservation of the protein points to another role of the gene.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of conservation despite loss of recombination function

claim: Partial PRDM9 orthologs share their domain architecture with other members of the PRDM gene family, many of which act as transcription factors.
source: In that regard, we note that partial PRDM9 orthologs share their domain architecture with other members of the PRDM gene family, many of which act as transcription factors (Hayashi et al., 2005; Vervoort et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hayashi et al., 2005; Vervoort et al., 2016

claim: The role of PRDM9 in directing recombination appears to have originated before the diversification of vertebrates.
source: Conversely, if the presence of all four domains, conservation of catalytic residues, and the rapid evolution of the ZF array are sufficient indications of PRDM9-directed recombination, then the role of PRDM9 in directing recombination appears to have originated before the diversification of vertebrates.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of complete, rapidly-evolving PRDM9 in diverse vertebrate lineages

claim: High allelic diversity is seen in the ZF within a python species (Python bivittatus), reminiscent of patterns observed in apes.
source: One hint in that direction is provided by the high allelic diversity seen in the ZF within a python species (Python bivittatus), reminiscent of patterns observed in apes (Schwartz et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5, with comparison to published data

claim: The intact PRDM9 has often been duplicated.
source: It further appears that the intact PRDM9 has often been duplicated, with more than one copy associated with recombination rate variation in cattle (Sandor et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis, supported by citations to Sandor et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2015

claim: Based on the RAxML tree of the SET domain, there are 55 independent cases of PRDM9 duplications.
source: Based on the RAxML tree of the SET domain, we count 55 independent cases of duplications.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's phylogenetic analysis

claim: At least six taxa of vertebrates carry only partial PRDM9 orthologs.
source: Although PRDM9-directed recombination clearly confers enough of an advantage for it to be widely maintained in vertebrates, at least six taxa of vertebrates carry only partial PRDM9 orthologs and the gene has been lost entirely at least three times (based on 227 orthologs; Figure 1, Figure 2).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figures 1 and 2

claim: PRDM9 has been lost entirely at least three times in vertebrates.
source: Although PRDM9-directed recombination clearly confers enough of an advantage for it to be widely maintained in vertebrates, at least six taxa of vertebrates carry only partial PRDM9 orthologs and the gene has been lost entirely at least three times (based on 227 orthologs; Figure 1, Figure 2).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the study's analysis and shown in Figures 1 and 2

claim: PRDM9 is not essential to meiotic recombination in the sense that SPO11 is.
source: Thus, PRDM9 is not essential to meiotic recombination in the sense that SPO11 is, for example (Lam and Keeney, 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of multiple losses of PRDM9, with comparison to SPO11 supported by citation

claim: In mammalian species studied to date, recombination rates are lower near promoters than in species lacking PRDM9.
source: In this regard, it is worth noting that in mammalian species studied to date, recombination rates are lower near promoters than in species lacking PRDM9 (Myers et al., 2005; Coop et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Myers et al., 2005; Coop et al., 2008

claim: PRDM9 binding motifs are strongly associated with certain transposable element classes in mammals.
source: Alternatively (but non mutually-exclusively), because PRDM9 binding motifs are strongly associated with certain transposable element classes in mammals (Myers et al., 2008), the role of PRDM9 in recombination could be related to the regulation of certain families of transposable elements.
evidence: Supported by citation to Myers et al., 2008
